audit_notes: Model: steady near-wall transport of diatom cells with a first-order wall reaction; the effective attachment velocity is the contact attachment velocity times the time-averaged survival under flow times the fraction of attached cells that consolidate before a thermal switch removes them, 1/(1 + p*t_c/t_s) (competing first-order processes: consolidation at rate 1/t_c, removal at rate p/t_s). Design: k_eff = 1e-4*0.45/(1 + 0.6*86400/43200) = 2.05e-5 m/s, Da = 0.102, J = 1.86e4 1/(m^2 s). Baseline silicone foul-release (p = 0): k_eff = 4.5e-5 m/s, Da = 0.225, J = 3.67e4 1/(m^2 s). Expected gain ~49 %. Energy check (not in the steady model): a pulse must heat the brush through a ~50 um topcoat (diffusion time L^2/alpha = 2.5e-9/1e-7 = 0.025 s) and loses heat to the water (h ~300 W/m^2K in port, ~3000 W/m^2K at 15 kn) and into the substrate (penetration sqrt(alpha*t) ~0.45 mm for a 2 s pulse). Per 2 s pulse at 15 K: ~10-15 kJ/m^2 in port, ~100 kJ/m^2 at speed. Two pulses per day: 0.35 W/m^2 (port) to 2.3 W/m^2 (at speed) average, i.e. 3.5-23 kW for a 10,000 m^2 hull, with ~50 kW peak for a 1 m^2 patch at speed; affordable for a ship's electrical plant, but it is a continuous energy supply and needs an embedded, insulated heater grid on the steel hull (cathodic protection, electrical safety, damage by fenders). Caveats: release probability 0.6 per switch and consolidation time 1 day are lab-level assumptions and set the gain; the brush ages like other molecular layers; the LCST must be tuned above the highest seawater temperature on the route (~32 C in the tropics), so heating to ~45 C is needed. Dimensionless: Damkoehler 0.102 (design), 0.225 (baseline); p*t_c/t_s = 1.2. Simulation coefficient: design k_eff 2.05e-5 m/s (informational).
